Time To Upgrade: Android Auto No Longer Works on Android 9 and Android 10
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Google
Android 9, also known as Pie and released in August 2018, and Android 10, which received the green light for production devices in September 2019, can no longer run Android Auto. Google has updated the list of supported operating systems for the car projection system, so if your device is running any of these two versions, the only way to still have Android Auto behind the wheel is to upgrade your phone.
We’ve known for a while that this was coming. Notifications that new system requirements were coming started appearing on Android Auto for some users in October, and now it looks like the change has been silently implemented.
The system requirements listed by Google now point to Android 11 as the oldest version of the mobile operating system that can run Android Auto.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The end of support Before you blame Google for leaving behind your ancient Android device, it’s important to know that moving to newer operating systems is required for new features and upgrades that wouldn’t otherwise be possible on old software.
With the migration towards AI everything, the switch isn’t necessarily surprising. Android Auto is getting deeper Gemini integration, with new features, such as Personal Intelligence, that will allow the AI-powered assistant to access data stored in other Google products, including Gmail and the Google Calendar, for personalized suggestions and answers.
As for how many devices are being impacted by this decision, the latest statistics shared in June 2026 show that 2.26% of devices were running Android 9, while Android 10 was still powering 4.1% of the Android devices worldwide. This means fewer than 1 in 10 Android devices out there are still running the dropped operating systems, so it’s safe to assume that not a lot of people will be affected.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution These numbers concern Android devices, not necessarily phones that are being used to run Android Auto. Android 9 received the last update on January 4, 2022, while the last update for Android 10 landed on February 9, 2023. Devices like Samsung Galaxy S9 and Galaxy Note 9 are, therefore, being left behind, as the latest OS version they received was Android 10.
The last time Google updated the system requirements was in 2024, when it dropped support for Android 8. Previously, Android 6 support was removed in 2022, so while many people expected only Android 9 to be left behind, Google is embracing a more aggressive approach and is dropping support for two operating system versions.
The new system requirements With this update, Android Auto needs at least Android 11 to run, no matter the connection method. The 2026 Android Auto wired system requirements mentioned Android 11 or higher and a high-quality USB cable.
These USB cables should allow for both data transfers and fast charging, as previously, finding the right cord for Android Auto was quite a challenge due to users unknowingly using charging-only cables to run the app.
You should always be using the cable that comes in the box with your phone.
If you want to use Android Auto with a wireless connection, assuming your head unit supports this connection method, you need at least Android 11 and “a compatible Android phone with an active data plan and 5 GHz Wi-Fi support.”
While these specifications could make you wonder if your device can run Android Auto wireless, there’s a good chance it can, as almost every new-generation smartphone meets these requirements.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution If your car is fitted with Android Auto wired but you want to use the app without a cable, your best choice is to use an Android Auto wireless adapter. Motorola MA1 and AAWireless are the most popular choices, as they connect to your phone using Bluetooth. They must be plugged into your Android Auto USB port in your car and then be in charge of receiving wireless data from your phone to forward it to your vehicle via the cable.
Just remember that running Android Auto without a cable can dramatically affect the battery life of your device. While this connection option would come in handy for short trips, such as when you go to pick up the kids from school, it’s not recommended to use Android Auto wireless without plugging in your smartphone on a longer journey. You could arrive at the destination with an empty battery.
Based on Google’s previous Android Auto system requirements update calendar, the next moment when such an update is supposed to take place is in 2028. At that point, support for at least Android 11 could be dropped, so be ready for an upgrade to a newer OS version or to get a new phone.
Google hasn’t released any announcement regarding the new system requirements, but considering the docs have already been updated, it’s safe to assume that the updated requirements are already in place, so your only option now is to upgrade your phone.
